MambaTrack: Exploiting Dual-Enhancement for
Night UAV Tracking
Chunhui Zhang1,2,3, Li Liu2,∗, Hao Wen3, Xi Zhou1,3, Yanfeng Wang1,4
1Cooperative Medianet Innovation Center, Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Shanghai, China
2Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou), Guangzhou, China
3CloudWalk Technology, Shanghai, China
4Shanghai AI Laboratory, Shanghai, China
Abstract—Night unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) tracking is
impeded by the challenges of poor illumination, with previous
daylight-optimized methods demonstrating suboptimal perfor-
mance in low-light conditions, limiting the utility of UAV applica-
tions. To this end, we propose an efﬁcient mamba-based tracker,
leveraging dual enhancement techniques to boost night UAV
tracking. The mamba-based low-light enhancer, equipped with
an illumination estimator and a damage restorer, achieves global
image enhancement while preserving the details and structure
of low-light images. Additionally, we advance a cross-modal
mamba network to achieve efﬁcient interactive learning between
vision and language modalities. Extensive experiments showcase
that our method achieves advanced performance and exhibits
signiﬁcantly improved computation and memory efﬁciency. For
instance, our method is 2.8× faster than CiteTracker and reduces
50.2% GPU memory. Our codes are available at https://github.
com/983632847/Awesome-Multimodal-Object-Tracking.
Index Terms—night UAV tracking, mamba network, low-light
enhancement, language enhancement.
I. INTRODUCTION
Visual tracking, a fundamental task in computer vision,
has received widespread attention in various unmanned aerial
vehicle (UAV) applications, e.g., aerial photography, target fol-
lowing, smart agriculture, and delivery. It aims to sequentially
track a moving object in a video from its initial location.
Despite signiﬁcant advancements, recent efforts have largely
concentrated on daytime UAV tracking [1]–[3]. Consequently,
numerous UAV-related applications are severely hindered due
to the insufﬁcient exploration of night UAV tracking [4], [5].
Generally, video frames captured at night have lower bright-
ness and contrast compared to daytime [2], [6]–[8]. To pursue
better tracking performance in the dark night, current works
mainly employ two strategies, i.e., low-light enhancement [9]–
[11] and unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) [4], [12].
Among them, ADTrack [11] is a pioneering anti-darkness
UAV tracker that adopts a tone mapping algorithm within
a correlation ﬁlter-based framework to enhance tracking ro-
bustness in low-light conditions. Later, some works proposed
to eliminate the inﬂuence of poor illumination by multiple
iterations [9] or a spatial-channel Transformer [10]. However,
these low-light enhancement-based methods either struggle
to preserve important local details of the image or have a
high computational burden. In contrast, UDA-based meth-
ods [4], [12] propose to learn from unlabeled data in the
target domain (i.e., nighttime scenarios), and utilize knowledge

performance in the target domain. However, these methods are
challenged by the imbalanced source/target distribution [12]
and limited data [13] for night UAV tracking.
To alleviate above problems, we propose an efﬁcient
mamba-based [16] tracker (MambaTrack), which includes two
simple and effective mechanisms, namely a mamba-based low-
light enhancement and a cross-modal enhancement. Owing
to the linear computational complexity of the mamba model,
our tracker exhibits signiﬁcant efﬁciency compared to state-
of-the-art (SOTA) methods (see Fig. 1). Inspired by the recent
success of state space models (e.g., Mamba [16]) in natural
language, speech, and various computer vision tasks, we intro-
duce a mamba-based low-light enhancer to improve tracking
performance in low-light videos. The low-light enhancer can
achieve global enhancement and preserve the local structure of
low-light images. Moreover, from a novel multimodal learning
view, we annotate language prompts for existing night UAV
tracking datasets [2], [4], [10], [11] for semantic enhancement
to mitigate the issue of limited nighttime data. This can greatly
reduce the cost of annotating massive dense bounding boxes.
In summary, the contributions of this work are fourfold:
• We propose the ﬁrst mamba-based baseline tracker for
night UAV tracking, achieving advanced performance
with high computation and memory efﬁciency.
• We present a mamba-based low-light enhancer (MLLE)
and a cross-modal mamba (CMM) network for image
enhancement and language (semantic) enhancement.
• We introduce a new vision-language night UAV tracking
task by adding language prompts for existing datasets.
• The proposed approach has been evaluated on ﬁve chal-
lenging benchmarks and has shown its effectiveness.

II. PROPOSED APPROACH
A. Input Representation
As shown in Fig. 2, the inputs for MambaTrack contain
video frames {Ii}N
i=1, and a language prompt S, where N
denotes the number of frames. In the visual branch, we crop a
small template Z from the initial frame I1 and a search area X
from the subsequent frames {Ii}N
i=2. The template and search
region can be enhanced using the proposed mamba-based low-
light enhancer. Subsequently, a linear projection is employed
to obtain 1D tokens Ho
z ∈RNz×D1 and Ho
x ∈RNx×D1, with
Nz and Nx denoting the length of the tokens, and D1 repre-
senting the token dimension. These tokens are then fed into the
visual mamba encoder to obtain visual embeddings Hz, Hx
of the template and search region. In the language branch, the
language prompt S is ﬁrst fed into a text tokenizer to obtain
language tokens. Similar to [14], [17], a class token [CLS] is
added to the beginning of the language tokens. Subsequently,
the language tokens are fed into the language mamba encoder
to obtain language embeddings Ht ∈RNt×D2, with Nt and
D2 denoting the length and dimension of the tokens. Finally,
we use a linear projection to transform the dimensions of
language embeddings to D1.
B. Mamba-based Low-light Enhancer
Based on Retinex theory [18], a low-light image I
∈
Rh×w×3 can be decomposed into a reﬂectance image R ∈
Rh×w×3 and an illumination map L ∈Rh×w, as I = R ⊗L,
where ⊗denotes element-wise multiplication. R is determined
by the essential properties of the target, and L represents
lighting conditions. Following [19], we introduce perturbations
to model noise and artifacts in low-light conditions, as follows:
I = (R + ˆR) ⊗(L + ˆL),
(1)
where ˆR ∈Rh×w×3 and ˆL ∈Rh×w represent perturbations
of R and L. Given a light-up map ¯L, with ¯L ⊗L = 1 [19],
we can calculate the light-up image Ilu as follows:
Ilu = I ⊗¯L = R + R ⊗(ˆL ⊗¯L) + ˆR ⊗(L + ˆL) ⊗¯L,
(2)
where R can be considered a well-exposed image and C =
R ⊗(ˆL ⊗¯L) + ˆR ⊗(L + ˆL) ⊗¯L is the total corruption term.
Eq. (2) can be simpliﬁed as:
Ilu = I ⊗¯L = R + C.
(3)
Therefore, the ﬁnal enhanced image Ien ∈Rh×w×3 can be
calculated as follows:

(Ilu, Flu) = IE(I, Lp),
Ien = Ilu + DR(Ilu, Flu),
(4)
where IE and DR denote the illumination estimator and
damage restorer, Lp ∈Rh×w represents the illumination prior,
Flu ∈Rh×w×d denotes the light-up feature map, where the
channel dimension d for Flu is 40. In our approach, Lp is the
average value of the channels [19] of the low-light image used
to measure the brightness of the image.
Illumination Estimator. As shown in Eq. (4), we feed the
low-light image I and illumination prior Lp into the IE to
generate a light-up image Ilu and its light-up feature map
Flu. Speciﬁcally, the low-light image I and the illumination
prior Lp are concatenated along the channel dimension, and
then fed into three convolutional layers. The ﬁrst Conv 1 × 1
is employed for preliminary feature fusion. The second depth-
wise separable Conv 5 × 5 performs feature upsampling to
obtain the light-up feature map Flu. Subsequently, we utilize
a Conv 1 × 1 for downsampling to derive the light-up map
¯L. Finally, we compute the light-up image Ilu as in Eq. (3).
Damage Restorer. The DR contains an encoder and a decoder
for eliminating noise and artifacts in low-light images [19].
The light-up image Ilu is downsampled using a Conv 3×3 to
match Flu’s dimensions. Two stages of downsampling follow,
each combining an illumination fusion state space model
(IFSSM) [20] and a Conv 4 × 4 layer. Similar to down-
sampling, upsampling contains Deconv 2 × 2, Conv 1 × 1,
and IFSSM layers. Deconvolution doubles the image size and
halves the feature dimension, and outputs are concatenated
with the corresponding stage of downsampling to mitigate

DR(Ilu, Flu), followed by element-wise addition of Ilu to

from existing works [11], [19], [21], our lightweight mamba-
based low-light enhancer is used to process the cropped small
template and search region, thus achieving efﬁcient image
enhancement with low latency.
C. Cross-modal Mamba Network
Inspired by [22], [23], we introduce a CMM network (see
Fig. 2) for vision-language enhancement learning. The core
idea is to map visual and language embeddings into a shared
space, utilizing a gating mechanism to enhance complementary
feature learning and mitigate redundant information, thus
optimizing cross-modal feature integration. We ﬁrst inject
language information into the search embeddings through
element-wise multiplication, as ¯Hx = Hx ⊗Ht. Then, we
concatenate the template and search embeddings to derive
Hvl = [ ¯Hx; Hz]. Similarly, we can obtain the corresponding
embeddings Hv without language injection. Subsequently, we
obtain hv and hvl through a normalized layer and a linear
projection as follows:
hm = Linearm(Normm(Hm)),
m ∈{v, vl}.
(5)
Subsequently, we compute yv and yvl via a 1D convolu-
tion [24], a SiLU activation function [25], and a state space
model (SSM) [16] as follows:
ym = SSM(SiLU(Conv(fm))).
(6)
Next, we calculate the reﬁned features zv and zvl through the
gating mechanism [26] as follows:
zm = ym ⊗SiLU(fv).
(7)
Finally, zv and zvl are added element-wise, followed by a
linear projection, and then residual on Hv to generate the
fusion feature Hvl = [ Hx; Hz], where Hx and Hz denote
language-enhanced search and template embeddings.
D. Tracking Head and Loss
We borrow the tracking head from [27], containing a clas-
siﬁcation head and a bounding box regression head. To speed
up model convergence, we adopt multi-task losses, including
L1 loss, GIoU loss LGIoU [28] and focal loss Lfocal [29],
and the total loss can be written as:
L = λ1L1 + λGIoULGIoU + λfocalLfocal,
(8)
where λ1, λGIoU, and λfocal are balance factors.
III. EXPERIMENTS
A. Implementation Details
Our experimental platform is a server with 8 RTX A6000
GPUs. We adopt Vim-S [30], GPT-NeoX [31], and Mamba-
130M [16] as visual encoder, text tokenizer and language
encoder, respectively. The template and search region are 22
and 42 times of the target and then resized to 128 × 128 and
256×256. The balance factors λ1, λGIoU, and λfocal are set to
5, 2, and 1.5. The visual and language dimensions are 384 and
768. The low-light enhancer is trained using LOL [32]. The
tracker is trained using the training splits of TrackingNet [33],
GOT-10k [34], LaSOT [35], COCO [36], and WebUAV-
3M [1]. We evaluate different trackers on ﬁve night UAV
tracking datasets, i.e., DarkTrack2021 [10], NAT2021 [4],
NAT2021L [4], UAVDark70 [11], and UAVDark135 [2]. For
fair comparisons, we primarily adopt tracking results of meth-
ods from original datasets [2], [4], [10], [11]. Due to the
absence of language annotations in these night UAV tracking
datasets, we manually annotate 518 language prompts (each
video with a sentence describing the class name of the target,
its attributes, and the surrounding environment) for multimodal
night UAV tracking. To facilitate future research, we will
release these language annotations.

NAT2021L is a long-term tracking dataset. Alongside algo-
rithms reported in original datasets, we evaluate multiple cur-
rent SOTA trackers, e.g., STARK50 [37], MixFormerV2 [38],
JointNLT [14], VLTTT [39], and CiteTracker [15]. Figs. 3
and 4 indicate that MambaTrack achieves the best AUC and
mACC scores among all compared trackers.
C.
Ablation Study
Component-wise Analysis. To explore the impact of the
two crucial components, (i.e., MLLE and CMM) in our
tracker, we conduct ablation studies on NAT2021 [4] and
UAVDark135 [2]. Our baseline includes only the visual
branch and the tracking head. We train it with the same
settings as MambaTrack to ensure a fair comparison. As
shown in Tab. I, our baseline obtains 48.7%/63.7%/51.3% on
NAT2021 and 51.4%/61.1%/54.5% on UAVDark135 in terms
of AUC/P/Pnorm scores. The MLLE module signiﬁcantly
improves the robustness of tracking in the dark, with AUC
scores increasing by 2.7% and 3.1% on two benchmarks.
The CMM module further improves the tracking accuracy by
adding semantic information, and the AUC scores increase by
1.8% and 2.7% respectively.
Attribute-based Performance. To comprehensively analyze
the performance of MambaTrack across various complex sce-
narios, we report attribute-based evaluation results in Tab. II.
Speciﬁcally, we use all ﬁve attributes from UAVDark135,
which are fast motion (FM), illumination variation (IV), low
resolution (LR), occlusion (OCC), and viewpoint change (VC).
The results demonstrate that MambaTrack outperforms all
compared visual-based and vision-language (VL)-based track-
ers on the ﬁve challenging scenarios.
Visualization. Fig. 5 presents the initial object box, search
regions, tracking results, and response maps of the video
Car1 from UAVDark135. The search regions indicate that
MambaTrack can concentrate on the real target in complex
nighttime scenarios, e.g., illumination variation and fast mo-
tion. This is mainly attributed to the proposed mamba-based
low-light enhancer, which achieves global image enhancement

D. Speed and Model Size Analysis
Inference speed and model parameters are two key con-
siderations since UAV platforms usually require low la-
tency and low power consumption [1], [43]. As shown in
Tab. III, MambaTrack achieves a real-time inference speed
of 42 frames per second (FPS). Compared with current
SOTA CNN-Transformer-based trackers (i.e., STARK50 [37]
and VLTTT
[39]), and Transformer-based trackers (i.e.,
JointNLT [14] and CiteTracker [15]), our MambaTrack re-
duces learnable parameters by 43.6% to 91.0%. Compared
with the current SOTA VL-based method CiteTracker, our
GPU memory usage is reduced by 50.2%.
IV. CONCLUSION
This work introduces MambaTrack, a novel tracker lever-
aging dual enhancement techniques for night UAV tracking.
MambaTrack utilizes a mamba-based low-light enhancer and a
cross-modal mamba network to improve tracking performance
in low-light conditions. Another signiﬁcant contribution of
this work is that we annotate language prompts for existing
datasets, constructing a new vision-language night UAV track-
ing task. Extensive experiments on ﬁve benchmarks demon-
strate the superiority and efﬁciency of the proposed approach
compared to current SOTA methods.
